scenes.text: The Great Wall is partly glued with rice.
scenes.visual: Bright summer day: the Great Wall paints itself up a green ridge; front and centre, a large blue-and-white bowl heaped with steaming sticky rice, with a big Ming watchtower (lookout roof, waving banner) directly behind it; a cloud drifts.

scenes.text: Ming builders boiled sticky rice into soup,
scenes.visual: Dawn at a builders' camp: a big iron wok set in a mud-brick stove, fire in its mouth, full of white rice soup, a wooden paddle stirring slowly, steam rising; a worker stands beside it; the wall is a faint line on the far hills. Note 'sticky rice' points at the soup. A rice sack and a basket of lime lumps sit in the foreground.

scenes.text: then stirred it into slaked lime.
scenes.visual: Close on a wooden trough of pale slaked lime: a ladle tips in from the top right and pours a stream of cream rice soup; a swirl opens, then a wooden paddle stirs it slowly round; a sack of rice and a basket of lime stand in the foreground. Notes: 'rice soup' (red) at the stream, 'slaked lime' at the paste.

scenes.text: It sounds like a kitchen trick, but it worked.
scenes.visual: Close on the wall face: big grey bricks and pale mortar seams with specks of rice, summer sky and a far ridge above; one gap in the top course; a new brick comes down into its fresh mortar bed and a bead of mortar squeezes out. Note 'rice + lime' (red) points at a seam.

scenes.text: One Ming tomb was so hard, a bulldozer could do nothing.
scenes.visual: Clear day on a plain: a Ming tomb's soul tower (crenellated brick platform with an arched tunnel, red pavilion with a yellow double-eaved roof, the green burial mound behind); a yellow bulldozer rolls in from the right and stops with its blade against the platform, exhaust smoke rising. Rocks, a shrub and grass fill the foreground.

scenes.text: In 2010, chemists in China found out why.
scenes.visual: A big painted '2010' on a pale blue swatch, hand-written under it 'Zhejiang University chemists'.

scenes.text: A starch in the rice, amylopectin, keeps the lime's crystals tiny and tight.
scenes.visual: Two microscope views stacked: top 'lime only', big loose crystals with dark pores between them; bottom 'with rice' (red), gold threads of starch appear, then tiny crystals fill in packed tight around them.

scenes.text: The mortar sets tough and shrugs off rain.
scenes.visual: Close-up on one mortar seam of the wall in a storm: wet grey bricks, slanted rain, wide dark wet streaks and drops running down the brick faces and off the seam. Note 'rain runs off'.

scenes.text: Centuries later, dinner is still holding up the wall.
scenes.visual: Dusk: the Great Wall and its watchtower on the ridge, the banner still waving, warm low sun; then the whole picture slowly washes back into the paper.

scenes.text: Subscribe for how the past was built.
scenes.visual: Title card: a small bowl of rice, 'Sticky-rice mortar', sub 'Ming walls, still standing'.

youtube.title: Sticky Rice Mortar: How Did Rice Hold Up the Great Wall?
youtube.description:
Sticky rice mortar is real: Ming builders boiled sticky rice into a thin soup and stirred it into slaked lime, and parts of the Great Wall, city walls, tombs and pagodas were built with it. One Ming tomb was so hard that a bulldozer could do nothing. In 2010, chemists at Zhejiang University found out why: amylopectin, a starch in the rice, keeps the lime's crystals tiny and packed tight, so the mortar is tougher and resists water.
